text:
𝗜 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗺𝘆 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 $𝟳𝟬𝗞. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘄 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲.

 My first attempt was 10 years ago, a service company with co-founders. 
We failed. 
But I walked away with connections and lessons I'd only recognize later.

 A year later, I built another service company. 
Used the connections from the previous one, hired a few freelancers, put it all together, found clients, made it work, and sold it for $70K. Back then, that felt like real money.

 And here's where it gets interesting.

 I thought — damn, I'm good at this. 
𝗜 𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝘁, and now I know how the game works.

 So I started another company. 
And I didn't sell it. 
I burned through that $70K instead.

 The thing is, selling a company didn't prove I understand business. It proved that my accumulated experience worked in that specific moment — the right timing, the right conditions, and maybe some luck.

 Real understanding comes later. 
When you try to repeat the success, and watch it fall apart. 
That's when you finally see what actually mattered — and what was just circumstance.

 My next attempt was again successful. 
A self-hosted generative AI solution for document generation and validation such as loan agreements. Back in 2018, it was a thing and a European bank has acquired it.

 So what I'm saying is — don't fear failure. 
𝗙𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝘃𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁 — cracked the code, figured out the universe. Like I did after that first sale.

 When you're convinced you're a genius and then you screw up — that stings in a special way. 😅

 This story never ends. First you learn how to make money. Then you learn how to blow it. 𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝘂𝘁.

 Is there a way to stay realistic after success, or do we all need to burn some money first? 😁
